content: A thread to discuss this attempt at a solution of Kevin Buzzard's challenge.

The main rule for this repo is, humans are not allowed to touch the Lean code, you need to ask your agents to do it. More generally we want as much as possible done by agents with light human guidance - this includes discussions of significant changes to definitions, pr reviews etc.

So I am locked out of Claude until Sunday, but realized that codex has 1 month free trial, so kicked it off and asked to see if there is something to port over from your repo to mine. It said no, but will ask claude on Monday too.

I started very ad-hoc initially, but now I realize the major question for this type of work is whether to work from the challenge (root) file up, or from the leafs down to the challenge (root). The both have downsides:

  • root up allows the AI to accidentally "prove" from unsatisfable hypothesis.
  • from leafs down risks that correct statements are not usable in the next layer.

I have instructed my AI to prefer the second as its failure mode is less painful from my experience. I think your repo was built mostly root down which is great for scaffolding, but risky for filling in sorries.

Whichever direction one picks, expect the plan to change and don't parallelize too soon.

Those are called backward and forward chaining. I prefer backward chaining (from the conclusion) but then one has to strictly vet the assumed intermediate steps, I spend a lot of time on that and use multiple models. Forward chaining is also good if you give the AI a source to follow and you are proving a result you know you need.

makes sense. I can't vet the intermediate steps, because I don't know the math, so rather build on solid ground, but with some intermediate statement vetting backward chaining would actually could more efficient.

Another method which helps backward chaining is to ask the model, can you prove X by postulating an intermediate lemma (or axiom) which does not depend on any project specific definitions. I find that when this is possible the lemmas are more likely to be correct.
There are multiple paths to proving the challenge (one theorem has different proofs in Miranda vs Forster). Did you direct that AI to pick that based on experience or trust it to pick?

I started from Mumford's Tata lectures which was where I first learned about Jacobian varieties (it is more computational) and also Milne and Debarre (free online). But it looks like the agents were particularly influenced by Forster. But generally I suggested directions to pursue, not really remembering which books they came out of.
yes, Claude follows Forster a lot, but it also found out that Forster needs Stokes on manifold for something, while Miranda has an approach that sidesteps it, which allows us to skip formalizing it.

There are discharge plans for all the axioms linked to from docs/planning/ROADMAP.md,
so hopefully one can contribute now without deeply knowing the math.

I just opened 62 issues for all 62 axioms.
I also made a global tracker so we can count the progress.
I think it is possible to close Class 2b (8 axioms) quickly because they are pure differential geometry. I am going to work on those first.

Maybe it's already too late, but I'm wondering if it would be possible for those working on the project to track how much human time is being spent. If the project is successful, I think that's one statistic that people will be interested in. After all, it's supposed to be an autoformalization challenge, where the ideal amount of human effort is something like 10 minutes. People will want to know how far the project fell short of the ideal.

Yes, that is interesting, though the human time is ill-defined. I am keeping rough track and I think I have spent 10-15 hours on the project so far, not counting some infra work. As a check, the total session time was around 100 hours so the fraction human/agent seems reasonable.
I have now added a field to the PR template where submitters can give their own estimates.

BTW, I am also doing autoformalization and at present that takes >> 10 minutes of human time: assembling sources, deciding what the goal theorems should be, sorting through failed runs etc. One goal of the project here is to draw lessons for autoformalization.

FYI: a core definition changed (path analyticity), and a note on our change protocol.

My agent strengthened the piecewise-analytic-arc definition (IsAnalyticArc → IsAnalyticArcStrong), which retired an axiom (60 → 59) and landed the HI-0 developing-map bridge.

The spirit of the project is that agents do the work with light human steering — including judging when a change is significant enough to flag. For changes like this (core definitions, axioms, shared interfaces, soundness), the protocol is to open a GitHub Discussion so it can be discussed before/around the PR. This one — with the API change and a soundness lesson worth your agent's attention — is written up here.

Maybe it's already too late, but I'm wondering if it would be possible for those working on the project to track how much human time is being spent.

Yes, that is interesting, though the human time is ill-defined. I am keeping rough track and I think I have spent 10-15 hours on the project so far, not counting some infra work.

I will track it very high-level, but I am decidedly not optimizing for minimizing human steering time at this point. Reasons being:
1) the task is too large and uncertain at this point, so even if some steering can be replaced with more AI tokens, I feel 2 hours of my time (cheaper because I am not a math expert) + 100 AI, is a good tradeoff for me compared to 200 hours of AI time.
2) it is educational for me to observe the AI more closely and understand how and when it goes off the rails. There is a lot of general engineering room for improvement around working with 10k+ loc codebases, that is generally useful to me even outside formalization. I see a lot of losing track of the big picture and inconsistent goals, that allows me to think how to improve prompting and adding guardrails for the next autoformalization project.
3) the off-the-shelf tools I am using claude code and codex CLI are not optimized for long-tasks and large codebases AFAIKT, so they benefit continuous project management from me.

That said, while I am almost continuously monitoring the working logs and steer every 30min to 1 hour, I don't ever touch the lean code or provide guidance on the math (I can't even if I wanted, I don't know the math). I realize that doesn't make this for a great scientific experiment, but still an interesting open ended exploration IMHO.

Asked my AI to track the steering I have been doing in an .md https://github.com/rkirov/jacobian-claude/blob/main/human_input.md

Btw, looks like various AI researchers have tried to turn this type of workflow into a more systematic process and tool - see https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.05400, but I have not tried their tools (at https://github.com/YuanheZ/LeanMarathon), because I am more interested in learning how the naive approaches fail before reaching for the fancier harnesses.
I agree, the goal is not to minimize human effort at this point, it is for us to learn. Still, it's interesting to roughly track.

Rado Kirov said:

Btw, looks like various AI researchers have tried to turn this type of workflow into a more systematic process and tool - see https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.05400, but I have not tried their tools (at https://github.com/YuanheZ/LeanMarathon), because I am more interested in learning how the naive approaches fail before reaching for the fancier harnesses.

I agree, settling on an autoformalization harness would be good for us, since it would allow us to have more organized workflow and data collection. For now, I am using my own hand-rolled harness for Claude+Aristotle (ironically, also called Marathon). I have been meaning to try out the LeanMarathon harness you cited, but I don't have a Codex subscription.

I also agree minimizing human effort is not the goal. Human review will be necessary to check the definitions anyways, so we should be leveraging human input rather than trying to remove humans from the loop.

Happy to hear discussion about and suggestions for harnesses to use -
probably should go in another thread.

I also agree minimizing human effort is not the goal. Human review will be necessary to check the definitions anyways, so we should be leveraging human input rather than trying to remove humans from the loop.

precisely, planning ahead of time for making it easier for human review (which is inevitable) is important and my agent currently doing terribly on this. Currently pushing a bit more to close more of the headline theorems and remove already identified incorrect definitions, but afterward will spend cycles to align better with mrdouglas' axiom terminology as that has the most human-friendly scaffold as it is steered by someone who knows the math.

Aristotle just discharged two axioms today.
56 to go!

See https://github.com/mrdouglasny/jacobian-challenge/issues/25 for an example of how I claimed one.

Active project axioms in jacobian-challenge are down to 50. :tada: .
Liouville L2 & L3 → theorems (PR #96). The two deepest remaining
axioms, both now discharged:

  • AX_HyperellipticForm_polynomial_decomposition (L2)
  • AX_HyperellipticOneForm_eq_form (L3)

Together: the classical canonical-differentials theorem for even-genus
hyperelliptic curves y²=f(z), deg f = N even — every holomorphic 1-form is
c·zᵏ dz/y with k < N/2−1. This backs genus_HyperellipticEven_eq : g = N/2 − 1.
Also landed

  • AX_pushforward_contMDiff / AX_pullback_contMDiff discharged (#88 @Deicyde)
  • PlaneCurve.instT2Space + topology cluster ported bottom-up to sorry-free
    proofs (standard-3 axioms only), retiring ad-hoc axioms (#94 @sqrt-of-2, #90 @Deicyde)
I opened a discussion #100 on the proof of AX_AbelTheorem.

I opened another discussion #103 and PR #105. This proposes inserting an intermediate, faithfully-defined layer between Buzzard's API and the classical mathematics. Right now Riemann–Roch, Serre duality, and sheaf cohomology enter only as opaque axioms (LineBundle, H¹, canonicalDivisor). The proposal gives them real definitions and states the key facts (RR, Serre duality, ∑ res = 0) as sorry-ed theorems — a self-contained sub-challenge, gated by a faithfulness spec that a degenerate definition fails. Buzzard's challenge then reduces to our axiom list and filling those sorries.
The design choice that makes it tractable: define H¹ algebraically via Weil repartitions (adeles) on the curve, instead of the analytic Dolbeault/Čech cohomology Mathlib lacks — which keeps everything curve-elementary and, crucially, keeps Serre duality a provable theorem rather than baking it into the definition. We only intend to fill this sub-challenge for curves (one-dimensional) — the adelic route is curve-specific by design and we are not attempting the higher-dimensional sheaf-cohomology generality.
@Michael R Douglas When do you estimate completition? The impression I get from your posts is that this is moving steadily along at a solid pace, but maybe I misunderstand.

Interesting, would it make sense then to target the alggeo version of the challenge in one big swoop? I thought switching between diffgeo and alggeo is non-trivial and needs large proof itself, just based on the fact that it’s a named paper GAGA.

Well, GAGA is a very general result, making the relation or switch in special cases can be easier. I had understood the foundations of what we are doing as algebra and single complex variables and not differential geometry. So this proposal made sense to me, but maybe it requires more careful look, that is why I put it up for discussion.

@Jason Rute, my guess at the moment is that we can fill 3 axioms a day so we could finish in 3 weeks, but there could still be a major blocker or buried mistaken definition which would prolong it. I do think it is doable but too early to promise when.

My agent is grinding in the mines of dolbeault/cech homology and getting kinda stuck (again only for curves but still looks tricky) so if algebraic path is shorter that would be nice. Someone should prototype it with some real lean.
Those do sound hard.

Re PR #108, this reduces an axiom to a sorry. There are some sorrys in the project which are not involved in the proofs for Buzzard's challenge but rather in constructing the hyperelliptic odd concrete examples. I am working on separating out this sort of thing.
I am doing the reorg of discussion #103 now, should be quick.

I finished the reorg. The project is now split into three parts: the original challenge, the proof of the required Riemann–Roch + Serre duality results, and construction of hyperelliptic surfaces with odd degree (branch point at infinity). I propose we focus on the original challenge and on making sure the RR/Serre axioms are properly formulated and adequate, and once we finish that we move on to prove RR/Serre.

BTW the agents try their best on docs such as README but they can do better with guidance, improving the docs is also a valuable contribution. Eventually we will want docs to help with the human validation, such as informalizations of results with cross refs to the sources. Note that the same policy applies to docs as to code (no direct human edits).

I just want to add a slightly cryptic "heads up" that multiple groups are working on the Jacobian challenge privately. I think it's actually fine and healthy, but I don't want anyone (here or in those groups!) to feel disappointed if someone gets there "first". There are gentle encouragements being made to publicly announce that you're working on the Jacobian challenge, but I don't have a strong sense of who will or won't do so.
It looks doable at this point, mainly a question of who throws the most compute at it.

Sure. I personally would feel a little cheesed off if I'd spent a bunch of my own money on it as a private citizen scientist (so to speak) and a lab with O($100k) of compute popped up with a surprise announcement, but then I don't actually have skin in the game. I guess we all know that's the gamble now, deciding to go ahead with a long (auto)formalisation experiment like this...

Thanks for the heads up. I was worried the ai startups were not interested, thus seemingly proving the claim that AI autoformalization is picking easier formalization targets, while our basic subscription experiments seem to point that this is not out of reach for AIs at all. I maxed out 2 weeks of Claude max subscription on this, but learned a lot about multi-agent workflows, autoformalization failures, general issues with agents working in 50k loc codebase, so money well spent in my book (also the subscription was already sunk cost, many weeks I just don’t max it out). We say math is about understanding, which should mean a little less obsession with being “first”.

Curious whether the full proof would fit in lean eval’s CI test time limits and what would be the human review plan after.

Michael R Douglas said:

It looks doable at this point, mainly a question of who throws the most compute at it.

I remain a little skeptical that this has been established. :-)

On my end I'm just happy to experiment and learn, the journey interests me more than the destination.
But I do hope we get there "first" as Michael has been doing such an amazing job at organizing the community efforts, and guiding less experimented hobbyist like myself, so thank you very much for this !
Update — RR + Serre are now theorems over a small cohomology scaffold. Proving them retired 5 axioms and added 7, landing at 43, with the new 7 vetted per-axiom by Gemini and Codex.

Opus 4.8 spend 2 good full days grinding (/goal works great, just learned about it) and the agent claims to have managed to get a sorry-free version of residue theorem for curves using tons of diffgeo machinery (mostly following Forster) - https://github.com/rkirov/jacobian-claude. ~57k lines of Lean (using cloc) across 277 files, 13min CI build.

Feel free to point you bots and pull whatever fits in your scaffold. I am not spending much tokens on cleanup right now (some whole branches ended up dead, so prettifying something that might get pruned is a waste), but eventually we would need to clean this up if we want humans to be able to do some review over it. So feel free to massage the code as you see fit instead of isolating in a vendored directory. Though vendored has a benefit that you can pull upstream change easier, TBD if getting up to the next layer of the iceberg will force a change or not.
@Rado Kirov , I did get more useful material from your repo. Making good progress. Important and probably not too hard to prove: AX_pushforwardAmbient_preserves_lattice, then AX_pushforward_pullback.
any soundness issues, incompatible definitions reported by your agents?
No, I check for problems frequently to prevent such issues arising.

Last night I finished AX_PeriodCycleBasis and the remaining integrations and solved the original challenge. It looks like it passed lean-eval but I am still waiting for confirmation and the leaderboard before announcing on the main thread.
In any case thanks all for a stimulating collaboration!

An interesting followup is that there is a good case for adding another condition to the challenge, in fact one can construct an object which satisfies the original 24 conditions but is not the Jacobian (though it is closely related to it). The best condition to add is an "Albanese universality" statement as explained in the docs. It is only conditionally proven on a few more axioms, and completing this would be a worthy continuation.
Did you use the proofs from the other solution and/or use Fable?

Yes I used Fable when it was available. This was a collaboration with many contributions including from Rado's proof as documented on the readme. But I stopped taking from Rado's repo after he finished so as to increase the independence of this repo as a data point.

As for theorems, it seems to me that challenges like this should always aim for having a unique chacterization of the definition (up to equivalence) via a universal property or other unique defining property. So then the challenge is essentially showing existence.
Yes, I think that is a good rule, at least when it is known how to characterize the objects uniquely.

+1 in fact such challenges can be seen as an experiments whether proposed universal properties are really such, when a proof of uniqueness is missing. Formalization and AI make proof experiments (not just computational ones) cheap.
For example, I got the AIs to construct the counterexample object I mentioned above.

By chance, in this case is the uniqueness proof much easier than the existence proof? Could Kevin have proven the uniqueness property (that any two Jacobians are equivalent) before giving the challenge?

I think if one adds the universality property, uniqueness is easy. According to the AIs, proving it from the 24 conditions + a 25th genus condition to forbid the counterexample is possible but quite hard.
